articles.title_orig: Israel Election Live Updates: Polls Open as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.title_zh: Israel Election Live Updates: Polls Open as Netanyahu Faces Challenge Led by Eisenkot
articles.content_orig:
Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority, with Gadi Eisenkot the leading opposition contender
What you need to know about Israel’s election
Hello and welcome to our coverage of the Israeli elections. Polls have opened in the first election since the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, Israel’s subsequent destruction of Gaza, and the launch of its war with the US against Iran.
Most polling shows prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition will lose its majority in the 120-seat Knesset, but the opposition bloc will probably also fall short of the 61 seats needed to form a government.
For Netanyahu, 76, who has led the most far-right government in Israel’s history, the stakes are both political and personal. He is on trial for corruption in three separate cases, despite interventions from Donald Trump, who called for a pre-emptive pardon in the long-running saga and even wrote to Israeli president Isaac Herzog on Netanyahu’s behalf. The cases are ongoing.
It was on Netanyahu’s watch that Hamas militants broke out from Gaza three years ago to kill nearly 1,200 people, the majority of them civilians, on the deadliest day in Israel’s history. This election is widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership since those attacks.
The IDF’s globally condemned assault on Gaza , which has killed at least 75,000 people and been deemed a genocide by a UN commission , academics, legal scholars and Israeli and international rights groups, has left Israel a pariah on the world stage.
Three years of regional conflict followed the 7 October attacks, including this year’s war on Iran , which sparked an ongoing global energy crisis and has killed thousands of people, mainly in Lebanon and Iran.
What is more, under Netanyahu’s government there has been an unprecedented, aggressive surge of deadly extremist settler violence to bolster Israeli control in the occupied West Bank , as settler militants and their political backers – who have propped up Netanyahu’s government – exploited their seat at the cabinet table and expanded with impunity.
Indeed, settlement expansion has been a key feature of Netanyahu’s re-election campaign. However, it is also a driving force behind Israel’s growing international isolation, with many of its traditional allies condemning “settler terrorists” and announcing plans to impose sanctions.
Citing figures released by the Central Elections Committee, the Israeli newspaper Ynet is reporting that voter turnout in the election reached 16.68 % by 10am local time (8am GMT), the highest level recorded at that hour since 1981 .
Over 1.2m Israelis had cast their ballots by 10am, according to the data, a rise of 0.78 percentage points compared with the same stage of the previous election in 2022.
In Sanhedria cemetery in north Jerusalem , ultra-orthodox voters came to the tombs of revered rabbis before they cast their ballots. There was no question of which way they were going to vote: for the parties representing Ashkenazi and Sephardic ultra-orthodox . But some at the Sanhedria cemetery, the young especially, made clear they only would do so reluctantly.
Yair Shuker, aged 19, said only one issue was important to him. “ The election is about whether we will live by the Torah, or there will be no Torah . There will be a Jewish state or there will be no Jewish state ,” he said.
And for him - as with almost all Israel’s ultra-orthodox ( the Haredim ) - the critical measure of the state’s level of observance is whether the Haredim would continue have exemption from military service.
“There are some who study the Torah, and some who stand and defend the land,” Shuker said.
The exemption for ultra-orthodox religious students dates back to the founding the state, but has long been a sort of tension among Israeli Jews, all the more so since the 7 October attack in 2023 and the start of the Gaza war. Israel’s supreme court ruled in 2024 that the blanket exemption for haredi men had no basis in law.
In return for their support in keeping him in power, Benjamin Netanyahu promised the ultra-orthodox parties (the Sephardic party Shas and the Ashkenazi United Torah Judaism ) new legislation that would perpetuate the exemption, but has failed to deliver on that promise due to splits in his coalition. As a result both parties left the government, though Shas remained part of the coalition.
Whatever their feelings about Netanyahu, both would vote against a secular-led government led by the current opposition parties, which have pledged to end the exemption once and for all, and enforce military service if necessary.
Shuker said he did not trust either coalition, but would vote because he had been told to. “The rabbi has asked us to vote for Shas, so I will vote,” he said. A 23-year-old Ashkenazi ultra-orthodox, who identified himself as Yaacov K, expressed the same sense of disillusion mixed with duty. He said:
double quotation mark I’ll tell you the truth. To me and most of the people around me, we don’t believe in anyone .
If you’re asking me, I’ll never go and vote. But I have a rabbi and the rabbi told me listen, you have to go and vote. And if he says you have to go and vote, then that’s what I do. I don’t even start thinking if it’s worth it for me or not worth it for me.
The open distrust and contempt for Netanyahu, coupled with obedience and party discipline, could be one reason that the prime minister’s bloc has over-performed by a seat or two in past elections, compared to his poll numbers. That could be crucial if the pattern is repeated.
Azriel Zadok, a rabbi who had come for morning prayers at the Sanhedria cemetery, argued that the mass ultra-orthodox vote was essential to preserve Israel’s Jewish identity from “the left”.
“We have no problem with the secular. We pray for them, and we pray for the soldiers,” Zadok said. “ Our problem is with the leftists we are trying to decide for us how we should live .” “They want us to go to the beach on Saturday and they want us to marry outside our faith. We want to remain Jews,” the rabbi added.
The centre left is only a small part of the opposition bloc, and it does not propose to change the ultra-orthodox lifestyle. But the bloc is united on the insistence that the Haredim should do their part in the defence of the nation. It is the most divisive issue among Israeli Jews voting today .
According to Israel’s Hareetz newspaper , United Arab List ( Ra’am ), an Islamist party headed by Mansour Abbas, has filed a complaint to the Central Elections Committee, alleging that a systematic campaign has been launched to disrupt voting for the party.
In a statement, the party said police arrested several of its leading activists in southern Israel’s Negev region before dawn with no clear justification, according to Hareetz.
The party also said there is a widespread shortage of its Arabic-language ballot slips in several areas, including the cities of Nazareth and Shfaram in northern Israel. We have not yet been able to independently verify these claims.
About 15 million people live in areas under Israeli control. Just over 7 million Jewish Israelis and 1.7 million Palestinian citizens of Israel live within the country’s pre-1967 borders, known as the “green line”, and have full voting rights.
In the occupied West Bank, more than 500,000 Israeli settlers can vote. They live among 3.1 million Palestinians who are subject to military rule and do not have the right to vote .
In occupied East Jerusalem more than 230,000 Israelis with voting rights live among 350,000 Palestinians who cannot vote .
Two million Palestinians in Gaza , who live under Israeli military occupation , according to the international court of justice, also have no vote .
The Knesset, the Israeli parliament, has 120 seats, with lawmakers voted in through a system of proportional representation. No single party has ever claimed a majority of 61 seats, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions.

articles.title_orig: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.title_zh: China's economy is outpacing the US despite Trump's tariffs. Here's what JPMorgan says it could mean for your money
articles.content_orig:
Voting booths are seen at Supervisor of Elections Office in Orange County, Florida, on the last business day before early voting begins for the Nov. 3, 2026, midterm elections.
William Diaz has a mantra: His only political party is his Venezuelan community.
He doesn’t abide by strict partisan rules, and doesn't believe in only voting for Democrats or Republicans. He supported Republicans Sen. Rick Scott and Secretary of State Marco Rubio when they were running for office in Florida , where Diaz has lived for 37 years.
For these midterm elections, however, the Orlando resident hopes to make a clear statement: He does not support President Donald Trump’s immigration policies and is unhappy with how Republican-backed initiatives have affected his community.
Read More: An Idaho ICE Raid Rounded Up Hundreds. The Fallout Could Change How ICE Operates
“I voted already, and what I did when I was voting and when I was with my ballot, I was really thinking and praying for all those that has no voice, those that can not vote, those immigrants that are right now victim of actions on the streets,” Diaz tells TIME, referring to Trump’s mass deportation agenda and the expansive influence of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). “My people have been suffering that much.”
Diaz is one of more than 2.6 million people who have already cast ballots in Florida, either by mail or through in-person early voting, according to state figures released Sunday. In-person early voting began in some counties Oct. 19 and expanded statewide Oct. 24.
Diaz’s community is one part of a Florida Latino electorate with varied national origins and political loyalties. Taken together, however, Latino voters are a swing vote in several closely watched races statewide. They were key to Trump’s Florida victory in 2024, with 56% supporting him over Kamala Harris, according to the 2024 American Electorate Voter Poll .
But new polls ahead of Election Day suggest that Latino support for the GOP may be on shaky ground—a shift that could put Republicans to the test in Florida and shape the political landscape beyond November.
Dissatisfaction among Florida’s Latino voters reflects a broader national mood, according to Stephanie Valencia, a co-founder of Equis Research, an organization that studies Latino voting behavior.
Concerns about the economy and immigration enforcement tactics are fueling dissatisfaction among Latino voters, who “make up a huge part of the electorate in Florida,” she says, pointing out that both of these issues are “disproportionately impacting” them.
A Univision/YouGov poll, conducted Oct. 2–15, showed that 41% of registered Latino voters in Florida were “very or somewhat worried” that they, a family member, or someone close could be detained or otherwise directly affected by immigration enforcement, compared with 27% of Florida voters overall.
The same poll showed that 4 in 10 Latino voters in the state felt that their finances had worsened over the past year, with 70% disapproving of Trump’s handling of the cost of living in the U.S. That stands in comparison to a 63% disapproval rate from Florida voters overall.
Read More: Midterm Ad Spending Has Surpassed $10B. Where Is the Money Coming From?
For Johanna Chavez, a Dominican immigrant living in Kissimmee, Florida, the economy is top of mind.
“Many people are concerned about the economy and the price of gasoline … and then there’s the cost of rent, it’s become incredibly, overwhelmingly high,” Chavez, who speaks Spanish, tells TIME through a translator. “All the things they promised would be done—nothing has happened.”
In the past few years, Chavez says it has felt like the United States has started “regressing,” and the opportunities she was looking for when she arrived here have not materialized in the way she had hoped.
“It’s starting to feel just like the situation back in my home country, the Dominican Republic,” she says. “We all came here hoping for change, seeking a better life, but it’s ending up being the same thing all over again. Things just aren’t what they’re supposed to be.”
Jared Nordlund, the Florida State Advocacy Director at UnidosUS, the largest nonprofit Latino rights organization in the U.S., says this is a common refrain among Floridian Latinos; people are upset over how the economy has been affected by tariffs and the war in Iran . Florida was hit particularly hard by rising gas prices after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz squeezed the global energy supply, he says.
“Florida is not a state friendly for public transportation, so people are highly reliant on the cars, and so what they would be paying for food now is having to kind of get broke between … paying to get the gas and then going to get food,” Nordlund says.
The question now is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Republicans—and whether it will be enough to tip the state’s close races.
Trump’s approval rating has plummeted with Latino voters in Florida, dropping from 58% approval at the start of his term to 36% ahead of midterm elections, according to Equis Research.
According to an AP-NORC poll from October, about 6 in 10 Latino voters disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency, and more than 7 in 10 disapprove of how he is handling the economy.
A Pew Research Center poll found that Trump’s job approval rating among Latino voters dropped from 38% in February 2025 to 24% in September and October. Of those who backed him in the last election, approval dropped to 57%—down from 93% in early 2025.
The shift may be resonating with Republicans like Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who is seeking re-election in Florida’s 27th District in Miami-Dade—a majority Latino district that Trump carried by some 15 points in 2024. She publicly broke with Trump in her campaign and criticized his immigration policies.
In one ad in September, Salazar said that Trump has “gone too far" with his deportation agenda.
“In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record,” she notes in the ad.
“Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy,” Salazar continues, addressing Trump. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
Guillermo Grenier, a Cuban American professor of sociology at Florida International University (FIU), agrees that many Latino voters are “ticked off” at Trump.
“The population, if you look at the whole Latino conglomerate, is turned off pretty strongly with Trump,” he says.
But South Florida’s Latino electorate is unique; Grenier points out that the state is home to 1.9 million Cuban Americans—the largest concentration in the United States.
As a voting bloc, the community has significant sway. In 2024, FIU’s Cuba poll found that 68% of likely Cuban American voters in Miami-Dade County supported Trump, compared to 23% for Harris—representing his highest-recorded support level in the poll's history.
A shift away from Republicans among Cuban American voters could therefore have significant consequences in South Florida. But disillusionment doesn’t always turn into action, according to Grenier.
“I think a lot of Cubans are pissed off at Trump, but they're still Republicans,” he says.
The Democratic Party’s response to this potential opening may unfold over several election cycles.
“Democrats are going to be in a probationary period with Latinos and with all voters, quite frankly, on whether they can deliver or not,” Valencia says. “One election is not durable support among a particular group.”
The electorate’s age also matters to its long-term political influence, says Michael McDonald, a professor of political science at the University of Florida. “Latinos are much younger than the rest of the population in the United States.”
He points out that voter turnout “is highly correlated with age” and expects Latino participation to increase as younger voters grow older. In his assessment, that could reshape the electoral map beyond

articles.title_orig: Here's the cash windfall the Anthropic IPO may bring to banks like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley
articles.title_zh: Here's the cash windfall the Anthropic IPO may bring to banks like Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan and Morgan Stanley
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
It stands to be a bountiful holiday quarter for some of the world's biggest banks, courtesy of the gift-giving team at Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ).
Using the SpaceX IPO fee rate, allocations, and a range of potential proceeds, EvercoreISI analyst Glenn Schorr estimates Anthropic's offering could generate a roughly $562 million equity capital markets (ECM) fee pool. That would equal about 1% of fourth-quarter consensus EPS across the banks he covers.
In Schorr's base case, co-lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley would each haul in $112 million in fees. Bank of America, Citigroup, and JPMorgan would each rake in $84 million.
A total of 22 banks appear on Anthropic's IPO tombstone, an advertisement recognizing the investment banks and other financial firms helping take the company public.
"A successful listing could also encourage more AI companies to test the public markets, accelerate broader IPO momentum, and reinforce the view that the AI trade still has room to run," Schorr added.
Anthropic's first-half 2026 revenue surged to $16.3 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier, the prospectus shows. The filing also discloses an $80.7 billion first-half net loss, a strong signal of aggressive AI spending in the years ahead.
Investment bankers are reportedly aiming for an astronomical listing valuation of roughly $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.
Anthropic could debut on public markets before the end of November.
"I think this needs to be valued appropriately," Manhattan Ventures co-founder Jare Carmel said on Sozzi Unleashed . Manhattan Venture Partners is an investor in Anthropic. "I think the biggest problem that we've seen in the IPO markets over the last few years are sort of valuations that have been offsides. And this needs to be valued to sell the IPO buyer, whether that's institutional or retail. They seem to hop around, especially when they're not getting the pop that they need. And I can fully understand why a company like Anthropic wouldn't would want to value themselves fairly as opposed to, let's say, undervalued. But the reality is you need to have shareholders for the long term."
Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title_orig: iPhone Duo: Apple says it will replace handsets with screen problems
articles.title_zh: iPhone Duo: Apple says it will replace handsets with screen problems
articles.content_orig:
Apple has acknowledged some of its iPhone Duo handsets have developed problems with their screens, just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.
Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device , which has a starting price of £1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.
Apple said it was aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.
The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, is an attempt to reinvigorate the brand's device range and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.
Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.
An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.
The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using AI.
Francisco Jeronimo, technology analyst at market research firm IDC, said that meant some caution was needed before drawing conclusions about the whole production run.
But he added the early reports of issues also showed "that even a company with Apple's engineering resources and supply chain discipline faces a steep learning curve in foldables".
The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in similar flaws in folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.
Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.
Android users already have a broad selection of foldable phones to choose from, technology that Apple spent years developing before the Duo's release.
It is Apple's most expensive iPhone ever, costing up to £3,199 for the most well-equipped models.
Jeronimo said because Apple had positioned the Duo as a "premium alternative" to established foldables, "how it handles this first-generation issue will shape buyer confidence in the category well beyond its own sales".
"Apple has a loyal customer base and a retail network that can swap devices on the spot, but with a further 28 markets launching on 30 October, it needs to clarify its warranty position quickly," he said.
The Duo marks Apple's first major iPhone redesign in almost two decades and was unveiled by new chief executive John Ternus, who took over from Tim Cook in September.
When closed, the Duo looks like a wider version of an iPhone, then opens up to a device resembling a small tablet computer.
"Others have created foldables that just feel like two phones awkwardly stuck together", Ternus told an audience at Apple's California headquarters last month.
The Duo, he said, would "redefine the experience of using a foldable phone".

articles.title_orig: Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
articles.title_zh: Israel election results 2026: When will we know who won and what’s next?
articles.content_orig:
Israelis are voting in a closely watched election to decide on the direction of the country, three years after the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on southern Israel that set off the genocidal war on Gaza.
The first election since those attacks comes at a time when Israel’s pogroms in the occupied West Bank have escalated, and amid mounting tensions with several of its neighbours, many of whom it has attacked in the past three years.
But the vote also comes amid growing domestic questions that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces over alleged failures that allowed the October 7 attack, his government’s handling of efforts to retrieve captives taken to Gaza, alleged corruption and disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service .
In final polls published Friday, Netanyahu’s coalition is expected to be neck and neck with – or trail slightly behind – the opposition bloc led by former Israeli military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot.
According to Israeli news outlet Haaretz, which has collated polls from Israeli news channels, as of Friday, an average of Channels 11, 12 and 13 predicts Netanyahu’s bloc will win 50 seats while Eisenkot’s opposition bloc will take 54 seats. The Israeli parliament, known as the Knesset, has 120 seats in all, so 61 is the mark that a grouping needs to reach a majority.
Here’s what you need to know about the election.
On Tuesday, polls opened at 7am local time (05:00 GMT) and will end at 10pm (20:00 GMT).
About 7.3 million Israelis will be eligible to vote, including 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel. Israelis living abroad cannot vote because the country does not have a general absentee ballot, requiring voters to be physically present on election day.
Diplomats and state emissaries are the exception and cast their ballots at Israeli missions on October 20.
News channels will broadcast exit poll results once the election ends, with the first indications likely within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or weeks to get a clear result.
Results will also be live on the Central Elections Committee website once polls close.
While a clear picture of the election results may come out quickly, if no party or coalition secures a majority, it could take much longer.
The final vote tally is expected by Friday, and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.
Under a proportional representation system, Israelis vote for a single party, not individual candidates.
The number of seats the party gains in the Knesset is linked to the proportion of the vote it receives. For example, if Netanyahu’s Likud party secures 50 percent of the national vote, it would take 50 percent of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
A majority requires 61 of the 120 seats.
For a party to enter the Knesset, it must secure at least 3.25 percent of the national vote.
About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.
Once the final count is in, President Isaac Herzog will speak with party leaders about who they want as prime minister, then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.
The person nominated then has up to 42 days to form a government. As it stands, no single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks.
If no government emerges, the current cabinet, Netanyahu’s government, will remain as a caretaker government.
But before that point, whoever gains the most votes will have different options to assemble support from smaller parties, including forming a minority government or working with another political leader to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.
If all negotiations fail, and no grouping is able to cobble together a workable government, new elections will have to be called.

articles.title_orig: Israelis head to polls in first election since the October 7 Hamas-led terror attack
articles.title_zh: Israelis head to polls in first election since the October 7 Hamas-led terror attack
articles.content_orig:
Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:
Voter turnout in the first three hours of the Israeli general election was the highest in decades, Israel 's Central Elections Committee said on Tuesday.
According to the committee, nationwide turnout by mid-morning was already at 16.68%, the highest at this stage of the vote since 1981 and up from 15.9% at the same time in the 2022 election.
"By 10 a.m., more than 1,200,000 Israelis had voted," said the committee's acting director general, Dean Livne.
Total voter turnout in Israeli general elections approached 80% the 1990s but hasn't been higher than 72.3% since the turn of the century. Turnout at the last general election in 2022 was 70.6%.
Turnout among Arab Israelis is expected to be particularly important given the role Arab parties could play as potential kingmakers in coalition talks.
"Our vote will change the government," predicted Mansour Abbas, head of the Islamist Ra'am party as he cast his vote, adding that he hoped turnout would surpass 70% in Arab communities.
Arabs in Israel make up about 18% of the electorate, and pre-election surveys have suggested a sharp increase in voter participation.
Data from the Midgam Research Institute cited by the Qatar -owned The New Arab indicates that turnout within the Arab community could rise to between 62% and 63%, up from approximately 53% in previous elections. The National , based in the United Arab Emirates , said its sources were predicting an "astronomical" Arab turnout.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Around 7.3 million Israelis (including around 1.2 million Palestinian citizens of Israel) are eligible to vote on Tuesday.
More than 640,000 young Israelis will be eligible to vote in a general election for the first time.
Around 3.1 million Palestinians living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank do not have the right to vote in Israeli elections, but 500,000 illegal settlers in those territories do.
A further 350,000 Palestinians live in Israeli-occupied East Jerusalem and also cannot vote, whereas around 230,000 Israelis living there can.
The US-based non-profit America-Israel Democracy Coalition (AID Coalition) has organized a "Fly&Vote" initiative, with as many as 67,000 voters returning to Israel to participate in the election, based on surveys of expatriates and registration data.
The coalition said half are coming from the US, with others from Europe, Canada, Australia and New Zealand. Israel does not have postal voting.
Israel is a parliamentary democracy and voters elect a legislature rather than choosing their prime minister directly. Voters choose a party "list."
Israel uses a proportional representation system under which 120 parliamentary seats are distributed roughly in proportion to a party's share of the vote.
To enter parliament (known as the Knesset), parties must receive at least 3.25% of valid votes, which is equivalent to roughly four seats.
The party which can command a majority of at least 61 seats is called upon to form a government. No single party has ever won an outright majority, so Israel has always been governed by coalitions. Polls suggest this year will be no different.
Unlike many other democracies around the world, Israel is not divided up into geographic electoral districts.
Rather than electing individual lawmakers to represent local areas, voters in Tel Aviv, Jerusalem and Haifa all choose from the same party lists in one, single, nationwide constituency.
When polling stations close at 10 p.m. local time (9 p.m. CET), broadcasters will publish their first exit polls, offering an initial indication of the results. Official results are scheduled to be published on November 4.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
While the main competition for the largest number of seats is between Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud and Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, the Arab parties are projected to play a key role in determining Israel's next ruling coalition.
For a party or coalition to rule, it needs to secure 61 seats in the Knesset.
As per a recent Channel 12 poll, Eisenkot's bloc is hovering around 55 seats, while Netanyahu's bloc is trailing behind with some 51 seats. This means that either bloc would need to form coalitions in order to rule, should the election results come out similar to the polls.
The most likely parties to tip the scales are the Joint List (projected to win around 9 seats) and the Ra'am (projected to win around 5 seats). The Arab minority, who are Palestinian by heritage but Israeli by nationality, make up around a fifth of Israel's eligible voters. Polls suggest a higher turnout rate for the Arab voters than seen in previous elections.
Netanyahu's Likud and Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudi parties attempted last month to ban the Joint List and Ra'am from running in the race, but Israel's Supreme Court reversed the parties' disqualification earlier in October.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu have ruled out an alliance with the Arab parties. But analysts suggest such stances are not set in stone and can shift amid coalition talks, a move Netanyahu himself has resorted to in the past.
The Israeli general election is considered by many to be a verdict on the country's longest-serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu .
But who is the opposition, and what do they stand for?
The main opposition force is a so-called "change bloc," a mixed group of center-right and some left-wing parties led by the newly formed Yashar (honesty) party and its leader Gadi Eisenkot.
A relative political newcomer, Eisenkot is the son of Moroccan immigrants who rose to become the chief of the staff of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) between 2015 and 2019.
Eisenkot has positioned himself squarely in opposition to Netanyahu in terms of his personality — an unpolished man of the people in contrast to the highly stylized and controlling prime minister.
Campaigning on accountability, political reform, and national unity, Eisenkot has sharply criticized Netanyahu's leadership before and after the October 7 Hamas attacks.
But his politics don't differ massively and, although he has emphasized equal rights for all Israeli citizens, he has been ambiguous on the idea of a two-state solution since October 7.
While backing Israel's military operations, he argues the government lacks a clear strategy and has called for an independent inquiry into the failures surrounding the attacks. His military record and the death of his son in the Gaza war have strengthened his standing among many voters
The parties in Eisenkot's bloc all have ideological differences but are united by their goal of removing Netanyahu from power.

Voting began in Israel at 7 a.m. local time (6 a.m. CET) on Tuesday in the first general election since the deadly Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, and the devastating war in Gaza unleashed by Israel in response.
Some 7.3 million Israeli citizens are eligible to vote, with polls showing a bloc led by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , the country's longest-serving premier, neck and neck with Gadi Eisenkot's centrist opposition alliance.
Most polling stations will close at 10 p.m. local time (8 p.m. UTC).
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.
Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu .

articles.title_orig: UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
articles.title_zh: UK prosecutors charge two after RAF Fairford incident
articles.content_orig:
British prosecutors say they ⁠⁠have charged two men with ‌‌offences under the National Security Act following an incident ⁠⁠in September ⁠⁠at RAF Fairford, an ⁠⁠airbase in England used ⁠⁠by ⁠⁠the United States.
British-Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said. They are due to appear in court later on Tuesday.
Abdulkarim is charged with assisting Iran’s intelligence service, and Essghir with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom.
The airbase in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, had been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran this year.
Essghir was arrested outside the base on September 27, when armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Dozens of residents were evacuated from their homes as police and army bomb-disposal experts searched for explosives.
Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men have been arrested and released on bail as investigations continue.
Shortly after the incident at the base, US B-1 bombers were withdrawn from the site.
Assistant Commissioner Laurence ‌Taylor, head of the UK Counter Terrorism Policing, said police believed ‌the country ‌Abdulkarim was assisting was Iran.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham last week said the activity at RAF Fairford was likely to have been coordinated in Iran, which Iran’s ambassador to the UK has denied.
Last year the UK said there had been 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK.
In July, Britain used new powers to ban support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and a linked group, Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which had claimed responsibility for seven attacks earlier this year at locations linked to Jewish and Israeli communities, and Persian-language media.

articles.title_orig: Deadly Russian ballistic missile attack hits Kyiv university, bridge, medical centers
articles.title_zh: Deadly Russian ballistic missile attack hits Kyiv university, bridge, medical centers
articles.content_orig:
Help us keep bringing the truth to light, even when Russia turns the lights out.
Russian ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a deadly attack overnight on Oct. 26-27, striking a university campus, a major bridge, an administrative building, and medical facilities.
Kyiv, a city of three million people, has been relentlessly assaulted by Russian ballistic missiles in recent months as Moscow exploits Ukraine's air defense shortage. While its battlefield offensive has slowed, Russia has chosen a strategy of mass aerial strikes against vulnerable civilians.
At least one person was killed, and 15 people have been injured in the latest Russian attack , Ukraine's State Emergency Service (DSNS) said. Those injured in the attack include a paramedic, a medical technician, and a 20-year-old university student.
The mayor later reported a strike on the city's Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River, one of Kyiv's major traffic arteries. The bridge connects the city's eastern and western sides and is crucial for the daily commutes of hundreds of thousands of residents.
The bridge and metro infrastructure were damaged overnight, Klitschko said. Train service on the bridge has been temporarily suspended.
Ihor, who lives on the east bank of the Dnipro River but works on the west bank, said his commute now takes around two hours, including about half an hour spent walking across the Southern Bridge.
"We’ll have to walk like this every morning now. Taking a detour would take too long," Ihor, who declined to give his surname, told the Kyiv Independent.
Iryna was also crossing the bridge while it remained closed to traffic, but she was using an electric scooter to get across. Following the overnight attack on Oct. 27, this was her first time commuting to work this way.
"This is an alternative means of transport, but I don’t know how long the journey will take," Iryna, who also declined to give a surname, said, expressing hope that the bridge would be repaired soon.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a university campus in the city was struck by Russia alongside Kyiv's well-known Kyoto park and residential buildings.
Education minister Andriy Butenko later said that the Russian attack damaged buildings and dormitories of the State University of Trade and Economics. He said there were no deaths among university students or employees.
"This is once again a terrorist country attacking educational institutions. A university, a scientific institution, a college, a school, or a kindergarten - the enemy directs its missiles at children, teachers, and scientists without any pity or humanity. There is no excuse for Moscow's cynical actions," Butenko added.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground first reported that loud explosions rocked the city in the Podilskyi and Obolonskyi districts at around 9:45 p.m. local time.
Just minutes earlier, Ukraine's Air Force warned that ballistic missiles and other missiles were headed toward Kyiv.
Explosions were heard near a metro station in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district, where a car was damaged, Klitschko reported .
Two medical facilities in the Dniprovskyi district were also damaged in the attack, Klitschko said. At one of the two sites that came under fire, blast waves shattered windows in the intensive care unit. Windows were also shattered at the other site.
A three-story commercial building was also "partially destroyed" in the district where one person was found dead, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) added.
A school building in the district was also damaged in the attack, the Kyiv City Military Administration wrote .
"Buildings of a university campus, dormitories, and nearby residential buildings were damaged" in the Desnyanskyi district, DSNS said .
Hours later, another wave of ballistic missiles attacked the city in the middle of the night.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground reported a new round of explosions at around 3:30 a.m. local time. At least seven explosions rocked the city in the space of three minutes. The blasts came minutes after Ukraine's Air Force warned that Russian ballistic missiles were bound for the capital.
Another blast shook Kyiv some 15 minutes later, without warning.
The second wave of missiles hit an administrative building in the Podilskyi district, Klitschko said . Non-residential buildings were also targeted in two other unspecified locations.
Some metro stations elsewhere in the city were damaged during the earlier attack, but were repaired by emergency workers overnight, the mayor reported.
Russia has attacked the Southern Bridge and other key bridges multiple times in October in an attempt to disrupt logistics and daily life in Kyiv.
Earlier in the night, Zelensky condemned Russia's attack on Kyiv and renewed calls for allies to provide Ukraine with air defense.
"Russian ballistic missiles struck the grounds of a university in Kyiv and the area around it — effectively the campus, Kyoto Park, the area near a metro station, and residential buildings," he said in a post to X.
"(I)t is precisely under such circumstances, when the threat is constant, when strikes can come at any moment and target cities and villages directly, that artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror," Zelensky added.
Russia regularly targets civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war.
Ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv in a fatal Russian attack on the night of Oct. 13-14, killing five people and injuring another 25.
At least one person was killed, and 24 were injured in another Russian ballistic missile attack overnight on Oct. 22, during which cluster munitions also targeted the city.
Volodymyr Ivanyshyn is a news editor for The Kyiv Independent. He is pursuing an Honors Bachelor of Arts at the University of Toronto, majoring in political science with a minor in anthropology and human geography. Volodymyr holds a Certificate in Business Fundamentals from Rotman Commerce at the University of Toronto. He previously completed an internship with The Kyiv Independent.
"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," said Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The highest number of casualties Ukrainian drones inflicted on the Russian military was recorded in March, with almost 34,000 soldiers killed or irrecoverably wounded.
Russia launched two waves of ballistic missiles at the capital overnight, targeting a major bridge, metro stations, and other civilian infrastructure.
Russian attacks hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge, disrupting metro services, as well as a university campus, an administrative building, and medical centers.
A ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid to enter the Russian occupied city began as Russian forces launched ballistic missiles at other parts of Ukraine.
Russia’s attacks on energy infrastructure, which weaponize winter to inflict suffering, amount to war crimes, a UN inquiry has found.
The attack is "part of a larger campaign of sabotage operations attributed to the Russian Federation in Europe," according to the Romanian Intelligence Service.
The investigation found that Russian designs for rocket-launched drones likely helped shape weapons China unveiled in 2025 and that Russian wind tunnels kept testing aircraft models for China's top arms maker after the invasion of Ukraine.
Ukraine used strike drones in an attack that took several hours near the city of Khrustalnyi, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova Plus.
"The agreement opens the way for an exchange of experience," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Fall as Traders Assess Iran Diplomacy, Saudi Attacks
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Fall as Traders Assess Iran Diplomacy, Saudi Attacks
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices inched higher Tuesday, reversing earlier losses driven by renewed diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war and hopes of a de-escalation in the wider regional conflict that has seen Tehran-backed Houthis target Saudi Arabia.
Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery rose 0.22% to $116.07 a barrel as of 6:23 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for June rose 0.52% to $102.29 per barrel.
It follows talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday, as they stepped up efforts to defuse tensions across the Middle East.
Riyadh said the discussions were aimed at keeping diplomatic channels open and preventing another escalation in hostilities. The four countries agreed to continue to engage to advance regional peace and security, according to Iranian state media.
The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.
Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reuters reported .
Prospects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices.
But earlier oil price losses were limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.
—CNBC's Justina Lee contributed to the report.

articles.title_orig: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts
articles.title_zh: Kyiv Ballistic Missile Strike Kills 1, Injures 15 in University Area and Multiple Districts
articles.content_orig:
In brief: Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s university district, killing one person and injuring over 10, mostly students. Zelensky warned of further attacks and urged allies to accelerate air defense deliveries.
Russian ballistic missiles struck a university campus and surrounding residential areas in Kyiv late Monday, Oct. 26, killing at least one person and injuring over 10 others, most of them students, as emergency crews searched damaged buildings for people feared trapped under rubble.
The strikes hit the grounds of a university near Kyoto Park and Lisova metro station on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, damaging student dormitories, residential buildings, and medical facilities.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said nine of the wounded were hospitalized, including three in serious condition.
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that further strikes were possible as Russian Shahed drone attacks continued against the capital and other Ukrainian cities.
“There is extensive damage, and there are also reports that people may be trapped under the rubble,” Zelensky wrote on social media .
The Ukrainian leader stressed that the missiles struck crowded civilian areas where, he said, there were no military facilities nearby.
“Unfortunately, there may be more strikes coming,” Zelensky added.
At 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA) reported that the number of casualties had risen to 15.
“Overnight, the enemy attacked the capital with ballistic missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles] UAVs. As a result of the Russian Federation’s terrorist actions, damage has been recorded in three districts of Kyiv,” the report reads.
Of the 15 casualties, 12 have been hospitalized.
According to the State Emergency Service (DSNS), two fires broke out in non-residential buildings in the Obolonskyi district. Rescuers have extinguished both fires. Two casualties were reported in the district.
In the Holosiivskyi district, the Russian attack damaged transport infrastructure.
The university affected by the attack was identified as the State University of Trade and Economics (SUTE), located on Kyoto Street in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi district.
The institution, founded in 1946, is one of the capital’s major public universities, with more than 15,000 students across six faculties, according to its official profile .
The university specializes in economics, international trade, finance, law, information technology, and management.
Russia’s ballistic strike landed near a university dormitory, shattering windows and injuring residents, according to Klitschko.
The mayor initially reported that a 20-year-old woman was hospitalized following the strike near the dormitory.
In a subsequent update , Klitschko said most of the 10 people injured in the attack were students living in university accommodation. Nine were taken to hospital.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service reported damage to university buildings, dormitories and nearby residential properties.
KMVA also reported damage to a school building in the Desnianskyi district.
A paramedic and an emergency medical technician suffered injuries after their ambulance came under fire in the Desnianskyi district, according to the mayor. Their injuries were not considered critical.
A strike near Lisova metro station also set a private vehicle on fire, while nearby residential infrastructure sustained damage.
In the Dniprovskyi district, a three-story non-residential building was partially destroyed, with emergency workers discovering the body of one person in its basement, according to the State Emergency Service.
The destruction extended across residential, educational and medical facilities in the two districts.
Zelensky renewed his call for faster deliveries of Western air defense systems and ammunition, warning that delays were leaving Ukrainian cities vulnerable to further Russian missile strikes.
He said Ukraine continued to face a constant threat from ballistic missiles that could strike populated areas with little warning.
Under such circumstances, he argued, “artificial delays in providing air defense to Ukraine help terror.”
The president called for political agreements on defense assistance to be implemented promptly, stressing that Ukraine needed sufficient weapons not only to intercept incoming missiles but also to destroy Russian launchers.
The latest attack came amid an intensified Russian missile and drone campaign against Ukraine, with Kyiv’s residential neighborhoods, transport facilities, and civilian infrastructure repeatedly affected.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.title_zh: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput
articles.content_orig:
Modders have found ways to remove NVIDIA’s compute performance restrictions on several generations of GeForce graphics cards. What started with the RTX 3090 series has now expanded to RTX 40 models and even the older RTX 2080 Ti.
The modifications can nearly double the throughput of certain Tensor Core operations without changing the hardware or flashing a new VBIOS. However, this does not mean twice the gaming performance, and the GeForce RTX 50 Blackwell series has yet to receive a confirmed working unlock.
The research builds on earlier attempts to unlock restricted compute capabilities on NVIDIA CMP mining GPUs. Developer Zagitta adapted these techniques for GeForce RTX 30 cards through the open-source GPU-Unlock project, while work involving TOTORONG’s firmware payload extended support to the Ada architecture.
Instead of modifying graphics drivers, the tools change low-level GPU configuration registers before the NVIDIA driver loads, removing limits on the rate at which certain Tensor Core instructions can be issued. The changes are temporary and are cleared when the GPU loses power.
The reported results are substantial in specific compute tests. An RTX 3090 Ti increased BF16 matrix multiplication performance from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS, while an RTX 4090 doubled its measured FP16 Tensor Core instruction throughput from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. KohakuBlueleaf has also demonstrated an RTX 2080 Ti reaching 111 TFLOPS, compared with 59.9 TFLOPS before the unlock. That particular card was already physically modified with 22GB of VRAM, which is unrelated to the software unlock. Successful tests have also been reported on RTX 3060, RTX 3070, RTX 3080 and selected RTX 40 models, although support is not yet validated across every GPU variant.
These modifications primarily affect FP16 and BF16 operations with FP32 accumulation, alongside certain TF32 and FP8 workloads on supported architectures. They can accelerate AI tasks involving matrix multiplication, including LLM prompt processing and some image-generation workloads.
However, actual gains depend on the software being used. RTX 3090 reports show LLM prompt-processing improvements of roughly 14% to 36%, while token generation remains largely unchanged because it is often limited by memory bandwidth. Gaming performance is unaffected by these specific unlocks. Most projects currently target Linux, although experimental Windows implementations are also available. They are not risk-free, and unsupported configurations may fail to boot.
Some users are already asking NVIDIA to officially remove these restrictions from older GeForce products, many of which are no longer manufactured. That would benefit owners using their existing GPUs for AI workloads, but it raises another question for gamers. Cards such as the RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 already attract AI buyers because of their 24GB memory capacity, and improving their compute performance could make them even more attractive on the second-hand market.
So perhaps asking NVIDIA to remove these restrictions is the right call, just not at the best time. It’s hard to argue against unlocking performance on GPUs that are no longer in production and, in most cases, already out of warranty. But the GPU market is hardly in good shape right now, and making older GeForce cards more attractive to AI users could make things even worse for gamers. But can it really get any worse?
Source: RTX 30 Unlock (GPU-Unlock), RTX 40 Unlock (GPU-Unlock-Ada), RTX 20 Unlock (Turing Unlock)

articles.title_orig: China’s First Distributed In-Hold Dredge Pump Equipped Ultra-Large Self-Propelled Dredger “Xin Hai Jing 1” Delivered
articles.title_zh: China’s First Distributed In-Hold Dredge Pump Equipped Ultra-Large Self-Propelled Dredger “Xin Hai Jing 1” Delivered
articles.content_orig:
It's on us. Share your news here.
Posted on October 27, 2026
On October 23, the “Xin Hai Jing 1,” China’s first extra-large self-propelled trailing suction hopper dredger designed with distributed in-hold dredge pumps, built by Shanghai Zhenhua Port Machinery (ZPMC) for CCCC Shanghai Dredging, was officially delivered at ZPMC Qidong Offshore Engineering base. The vessel achieves full-chain independent controllability of dredging equipment—from overall design to core components—and combines intelligent operation with green, low-carbon advantages. It will support major marine engineering projects and inject strong marine engineering momentum into the building of a maritime power.
It is reported that this vessel was constructed under a turnkey contract by the National Engineering Research Centre of Dredging and designed by the Marine Design and Research Institute of China (MARIC). With a maximum hopper capacity of 27,929 m³ and a maximum dredging depth of 120 meters, the vessel’s performance, environmental standards, and technical capabilities all rank among the world’s best, marking China’s achievement of full autonomy and control over the entire dredging equipment supply chain—from overall design to core components.
The “Xin Hai Jing 1” has an overall length of 180 meters, a beam of 36 meters, and a draft of 17.2 meters. Breaking away from the traditional centralized layout of mud pumps on cutter-suction dredgers, it is the first vessel to install two in-hold mud pumps in separate forward and aft pump compartments at the front and rear of the mud hold, respectively. This innovative hydrodynamic layout addresses the challenges of pipeline resistance and center of gravity balance in ultra-large vessels under extreme operating conditions, significantly enhancing stability and dredging efficiency under various loading conditions, and filling a gap in the design and application of distributed in-hold dredge pumps in China’s dredging industry.
Full-chain domestic production is the most outstanding achievement of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” Centering on the requirements for ultra-large dredging depth, ultra-strong soil-breaking capability, and ultra-long discharge distance, all parties involved ine thconstruction adhered to demand-driven development and mobilized more than 110 domestic suppliers for collaborative research and development. Together they developed a series of core dredging-specific equipment, including a high-capacity, high-efficiency universal draghead suitable for both deep and shallow water, a lightweight 120-meter deep-water long drag arm system, and a high-efficiency hopper loading and overflow device. These efforts have driven a large number of core dredging-specific equipment items to complete domestic verification and supporting application, establishing a complete closed loop covering design and R&D, system integration, core supporting equipment, and full-scale ship verification, effectively shoring up shortcomings in China’s dredging and reclamation industry chain.
Intelligence and green development are the distinctive hallmarks of the “Xin Hai Jing 1.” The vessel is equipped with a new-generation intelligent monitoring and integrated management platform fully independently developed by China, adopting a “1 platform + N systems” architecture that enables fully automated control of “one-key dredging,” “one-key spoil dumping,” and “one-key reclamation,” and achieves “dredging-navigation integration” and even “unmanned dredging” under typical operating conditions.
Its digital twin system and “digital sentinels” based on AI vision and LiDAR can intelligently identify safety hazards such as smoke, flames, and oil leaks, with a recognition accuracy of over 95%. Both the main and auxiliary diesel engines are equipped with SCR denitrification systems. Through comprehensive measures including distributed in-hold dredge pumps, optimized pipeline layout, streamlined hull form for drag reduction, hybrid drive, and intelligent power and energy efficiency management, the vessel achieves a carbon emission reduction of more than 20% and a dredging efficiency improvement of approximately 30% compared with conventional vessels of the same type.
Once delivered and put into service, the vessel will be widely deployed for major projects such as deep-sea sand dredging, deep-water port and channel dredging along the coast, land reclamation, and coastal protection. It will further strengthen the capabilities of China’s ultra-large cutter suction dredger fleet and continue to advance the localization and iterative development of key supporting components, as well as the research and development of a series of related equipment.

articles.title_orig: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.title_zh: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers
articles.content_orig:
Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’
The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.
The lawsuit , filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardian investigation published last December.
“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” the 95-page legal complaint claims.
“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”
The lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.
The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.
Dollar General pushed back against the allegations.
“The lawsuit filed today ... suggests that we have abandoned our mission and willfully disregarded the affordability needs of our customers,” the company said in statement . “Nothing could be further from the truth. Our goal is 100% accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”
The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025 investigation , which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.
The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.
“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”
The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a former lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”
The lawsuit indicates that FTC investigators made undercover purchases at Dollar General stores in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Missouri and Maryland over a two and half month span. The first of these secret shopper tests took place this January, six weeks after the Guardian’s investigation focused wide attention on the discount chain’s pricing practices.
Every single undercover visit, the suit says, turned up overcharges on multiple products. At a Dollar General in Cleveland, eight of 58 items purchased rang up more costly than the prices listed on the product label or shelf – an overcharge rate of nearly 14%.
Dollar General said it first learned of the FTC’s investigation in February when it received a civil investigative demand from the agency. The company said that the investigation appeared to have “an unusually accelerated timeline” but that it “engaged cooperatively with the commission, producing more than 200,000 documents and over 350 gigabytes of data and making several company representatives available to provide sworn testimony on relatively short notice”.
The company’s statement said it pushed back against the calculations behind the FTC’s demand for financial compensation for consumers, but that it was surprised when the agency did not respond to its counteroffer and instead filed suit.
Dollar General said it “will defend this litigation vigorously”.
The company said that, in the retail marketplace, “occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement.”
In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James, announced earlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.

articles.content_orig:
US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.
The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa , has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China , Russia or North Korea .
Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.
American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.
In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.
China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.
It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan , where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title_orig: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.title_zh: From the Mediterranean to the dinner table
articles.content_orig:
Bluefin tuna does not forgive delay. The fatty belly — otoro — is prized for a richness that seems to dissolve on the tongue, a quality built on gloss, deep color and a marine intensity that no cooked fish can replicate. That pleasure lasts only as long as the cold chain holds. A few hours of warmth, a break in handling, and the texture turns from silk to something far less forgiving.
Delivering bluefin at its best is therefore an industrial problem disguised as a culinary one. The fish must move from sea to ultra-low-temperature storage quickly, in volume, and without interruption.
The Ocean Star exists for that problem. It is a floating cold-chain hub that links Maltese harvesting expertise with Chinese cold-chain capacity.
It is an ultra-low-temperature processing and transportation vessel owned by Mediterranean Bluefin Industry Development (Hainan), a China-Malta joint venture specializing in bluefin tuna processing and trade.
The joint venture was established in June 2024 by Malta Fish Farming Ltd, or MFF, and China's Shandong Far-sea Development Ltd, covering trade, transportation and processing.
The vessel began a new production season in late September, operating in the Mediterranean east of Malta.
Workers weigh tuna on its decks, move product into refrigerated rooms, and dock at Valletta Port — images that trace the journey from harvest to cold storage.
MFF Chairman Salvu Ellul described the Ocean Star as the first ultra-low-temperature refrigerated transport and processing vessel and said it had become the most efficient bluefin tuna processing platform in the Mediterranean region.
He made the remarks on Oct 11 while briefing China's Ambassador to Malta, Zhang Zuo, during a visit to the Valletta waterfront in October.
Ellul told the ambassador that cooperation between the two nations in the fisheries sector had expanded year by year and that there were high expectations the partnership would serve as a bridge for economic and trade exchanges between China and Malta.
Ellul pointed to the Belt and Road Initiative as a source of trade opportunities, saying that Malta Fish Farming would ride the wind and waves to bring Malta's highest quality bluefin tuna products to the consumers' table worldwide.

AI-generated “sob-story boys” have recently taken Chinese short-video platforms by storm, allegedly using emotional manipulation to cheat elderly viewers out of their savings.

articles.title_orig: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.title_zh: China and Russia are redrawing Arctic trade. Can Europe fight back?
articles.content_orig:
China and Russia are tightening their grip on Arctic shipping routes, turning the rapidly warming region into a new geopolitical battleground with Europe.
Moscow and Beijing last week have agreed to expand freight traffic along Arctic shipping corridors , increase services between their ports and deepen cooperation on building polar vessels.
The agreement came after the EU unveiled a new Arctic strategy aimed at countering growing Russian and Chinese influence in the region.
Although the competing moves underscore how the once-remote region is turning into a strategic prize, analysts said that Europe's ability to challenge the emerging China-Russia partnership remains limited, given Moscow's control over the main shipping corridor and Beijing's growing commercial clout.
That's because Moscow controls the Northern Sea Route, including shipping permits, transit fees and a vast fleet of nuclear icebreakers, while Beijing provides the cargo, vessels and industrial capacity needed to develop the corridor, she added.
Europe, by contrast, has limited icebreaker capacity and Arctic infrastructure, leaving it with little leverage to challenge the partnership despite its position as a major destination market.
The Northern Sea Route offers itself as an increasingly attractive alternative, as Middle East disruptions expose vulnerabilities in established shipping corridors.
Cargo traveling between Asia and Europe through the Northern Sea Route could have its journey shortened to between 18 to 22 days, down approximately 35% from the 28 to 35 day journey through Suez, according to data provided by Fertmax FZCO.
For Moscow, the route offers an opportunity to redirect energy exports toward Asia as Western sanctions constrain its access to European markets, said industry watchers whom CNBC spoke to.
On the other hand, it provides Beijing another trade artery that could reduce reliance on traditional maritime chokepoints.
David Roche, a veteran strategist at Quantum Strategy & Geonomics, said the Arctic's importance lies less in its potential to transform global shipping than in the deepening economic dependence between Russia and China.
"The significance of the arctic route is for Russian energy shipments to China, which will increase China's control over Russia in terms of Russia's dependence on China to sell its energy to compensate for losses of its gas markets in Europe," Roche highlighted.
The EU has acknowledged the growing challenge, highlighting the region's strategic value in its strategy, as mentioned by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas last week .
Europe isn't entirely without leverage.
The EU's new strategy calls for expanding European icebreaker capacity, strengthening maritime surveillance and developing infrastructure linking Arctic trade networks to European markets.
It also proposes a maritime security hub and greater protection for undersea cables, reflecting growing concerns about Russian military activity and threats to critical infrastructure.
Yet those strengths may not be enough to overturn the structural advantages enjoyed by Moscow and Beijing, said experts.
Garcia-Herrero said Europe's leverage largely rests on its position as a major destination market and the presence of large shipping companies that have avoided the Arctic because of environmental and commercial risks.
Europe also faces a strategic dilemma: engaging with the emerging corridor could deepen its reliance on Russian-controlled infrastructure, even as it seeks to reduce Moscow's economic influence.
Fertmax FZCO's former global head of research, Daeijin Lee said Western operators face sanctions, insurance and compliance complications that make the route considerably less attractive than it is for Chinese companies.
"The Arctic gives diversification, not independence," he said.
For all the geopolitical attention, the Arctic remains a marginal player in global shipping.
Roche estimates Arctic trade accounts for roughly 0.3% of global shipping today and could reach about 1% by 2030.
Data from Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom and CNBC calculations based on UN Trade and Development figures similarly supports the 0.3% figure, with 37.02 million tonnes of cargo transiting the Northern Sea Route in 2025 compared to the 12.72 billion tonnes of global seaborne trade in 2024.
Only 3.2 million tonnes of that cargo, or less than a tenth, involved vessels transiting the entire route, rather than shipments originating or terminating in the Russian Arctic, according to the Centre for High North Logistics .
But traffic may be picking up, the latest September 2026 CHNL data showed.
The route recorded 104 confirmed transit voyages carrying an estimated 3.7 million tonnes of cargo by the end of September, exceeding the 3.2 million tonnes recorded during the entire 2025 navigation season.
Much of the existing traffic consists of Russian oil, liquefied natural gas and other commodities rather than international container shipments.
However, the route also faces significant commercial hurdles. Ice conditions restrict navigation for much of the year, while specialized vessels, insurance premiums and Russian transit fees can erode savings from shorter voyages.
Matthew Wright, an analyst at Kpler, said the route remains poorly suited to replacing established shipping corridors because operators need reliable, year-round services.
Lee similarly expects the Arctic to develop primarily as a seasonal express route for selected high-value cargo rather than a replacement for Suez.
However, climate change could shift the balance in the long-term.
A study published in the WMU Journal of Maritime Affairs projected that melting Polar ice could increase the Northern Sea Route's annual transit capacity to between 127 million and 463 million tonnes by 2050.
